findings.claim: a Latin word for grain mush, long before corn arrived
findings.because: In classical Latin, polenta meant hulled barley groats or barley meal (Pliny, Columella). The Latin word for a grain mush was puls.
findings.fix: Northern Italy; Latin polenta meant barley meal, long before corn arrived

findings.claim: Grits are stone-ground corn slow-cooked until creamy
findings.because: Many grits are not stone-ground. Plenty of kitchens use quick or regular degerminated grits, and the why says so itself. A server who repeats this line may be describing the plate wrongly.
findings.fix: Grits are ground dried corn slow-cooked until creamy

findings.claim: light and pillowy, made by hand
findings.because: Whether gnocchi are handmade depends on the kitchen, and many restaurants buy them in. The card should not have a server promise this to a guest.
findings.fix: light and pillowy

findings.claim: Breton crepes
findings.because: The buckwheat dish of Brittany is the savory galette (galette de sarrasin). Breton crepes are the sweet ones, made with wheat flour. Galette is a card on the roster.
findings.fix: Breton galettes

findings.claim: Piccolo is einkorn, the first wheat people farmed
findings.because: Einkorn and emmer were both domesticated in the Fertile Crescent at about the same time, around 10,000 years ago. Sources disagree about which came first, so 'the first' is stronger than the evidence.
findings.fix: Piccolo is einkorn, one of the first wheats people farmed

findings.claim: The oldest farmed wheat
findings.because: Einkorn's claim to be older than emmer is disputed, because both were domesticated at about the same time.
findings.fix: One of the first farmed wheats

findings.claim: filled with roast meat
findings.because: Many kitchens fill agnolotti with squash, cheese or potato. A new hire who repeats this as fact will tell a guest that a squash agnolotti holds meat, or tell a guest who avoids meat that the dish is the classic one. The classic filling belongs in why and madeWith, and the guest line should frame it as the traditional version.
findings.fix: They're little pinched pillows of fresh egg pasta from northern Italy, classically filled with roast meat. Small, tender, made to soak up sauce.

findings.claim: light and pillowy, made by hand
findings.because: Many kitchens use bought or machine-extruded gnocchi. A server who promises they are handmade is making a claim the card cannot back.
findings.fix: They're soft little potato dumplings, light and pillowy. Think of the best mashed potato turned into bite-size pasta.

findings.claim: stone-ground corn slow-cooked until creamy, with butter and often cheese
findings.because: Not every kitchen uses stone-ground grits or finishes them with butter. The guest line tells the server to state what is in the dish, so a guest who avoids dairy hears butter as a fact about tonight's plate when the recipe varies. The dairy belongs in madeWith.
findings.fix: Grits are ground corn slow-cooked until creamy, often finished with butter. It's the South's comfort food, and great under shrimp.

findings.claim: slow-cooked with butter and cheese
findings.because: It is stated as fact, but many kitchens make polenta with stock or water, or leave out the cheese. The server would be announcing dairy as certain when madeWith correctly says 'often'.
findings.fix: It's Italian cornmeal slow-cooked until creamy, often with butter and cheese. Soft, it's like a savory corn pudding, and grilled it gets a crisp crust.

findings.claim: (no say given)
findings.because: New hires hesitate over bulgur: is it BUL-gur, bul-GOOR or BOOL-gar? American dining rooms say BUHL-ger, so the card should give that respelling.
findings.fix: BUHL-ger

findings.claim: It's the smallest and oldest of the ancient Italian wheats.
findings.because: The card's own menu line sells it as 'Einkorn risotto', and guests who read food labels know the word einkorn. The guest line never says the name a guest would recognize, so a server who is asked 'is that einkorn?' is left with nothing to say. Einkorn is also not originally Italian.
findings.fix: It's einkorn, the smallest and oldest of the ancient wheats.

findings.claim: del plin means with a pinch in local dialect
findings.because: The phrase is not introduced: the card never says that 'agnolotti del plin' is the menu name for the pinched style. A new hire reading it cannot tell where 'del plin' comes from or when a guest would see it.
findings.fix: Piedmont, northern Italy; the pinched style is agnolotti del plin, plin meaning pinch

findings.claim: Despite the name it isn't wheat at all, it's a seed from a plant related to rhubarb.
findings.because: A guest who has to avoid wheat will hear 'isn't wheat at all' as an assurance about the dish. The card's own note says soba, blini and many buckwheat crepes are blended with wheat flour. The botany can stay, but the guest line must not sound like a clearance.
findings.fix: Despite the name it's no kin to wheat, it's a seed from a plant related to rhubarb.

findings.claim: "buckwheat", "sometimes wheat flour", "sometimes egg", "sometimes butter"
findings.because: The card names blini and crepes as classic uses. Blini are classically made with milk, and many crepe batters are too, but the list never flags milk.
findings.fix: add "sometimes milk"

findings.claim: Not pasta dough.
findings.because: A server who says 'not pasta' or 'not pasta dough' at the table can be heard as saying there is no wheat, but potato gnocchi are bound with wheat flour, and ricotta gnocchi and alla romana gnocchi are made with wheat too. The contrast should be about shape and texture, not ingredients.
findings.fix: Not rolled pasta, though flour binds them.

findings.claim: Not pappardelle, which are about twice as wide.
findings.because: Tagliatelle are about 7 to 8 mm wide and pappardelle usually 2 to 3 cm, so pappardelle run roughly three times as wide. 'About twice' understates the difference a server uses to tell them apart.
findings.fix: Not pappardelle, which are about three times as wide.

findings.claim: Long-kerneled Italian risotto rice prized for its firm center
findings.because: Acquerello (fd_0183) is carnaroli, so this gist is equally true of Acquerello. If it shows up as a wrong option under Acquerello, a learner who picks it is right. The gist needs something only the variety has, such as its 1945 breeding, and nothing the aged brand also has.
findings.fix: Longer, firmer risotto rice variety bred near Milan in 1945

findings.claim: Brand of Italian rice aged a year or more in the husk before milling
findings.because: Next to the Carnaroli gist, which describes the same grain, only the word brand and the ageing separate the two. Put the germ added back in, which only Acquerello has, so it cannot be swapped with fd_0182.
findings.fix: Branded risotto rice aged in the husk, its germ milled back in

findings.claim: that the farm ages for at least a year. The grains stay firm and absorb flavor beautifully.
findings.because: 'The farm' leaves the guest asking which farm, and 'absorb flavor beautifully' sounds like brochure copy. Say what the ageing does in plain words.
findings.fix: It's a prized Italian risotto rice, aged at least a year before milling, so the grains stay firm and soak up the broth.

findings.claim: sold in tins, so ask for it by name.
findings.because: A guest never asks for the rice by name, so 'ask for it by name' gives the server nothing to do. What the server needs to know is that it is carnaroli from one estate.
findings.fix: Not a variety but a brand: aged carnaroli from a single Piedmont estate, sold in tins.

findings.claim: Semolina gnocchi, brown butter, sage
findings.because: Semolina gnocchi (gnocchi alla romana) are soft, baked rounds of semolina porridge. The guest line promises that semolina gives 'a firm bite', so a server reading it at this dish would be wrong at the table. Use a dish where the guest line holds.
findings.fix: Hand-rolled semolina cavatelli, sausage, broccoli rabe

findings.claim: the backbone of dried pasta. It gives pasta and bread a firm bite and a sunny color.
findings.because: 'Backbone' and 'sunny color' read like copy off a card, not something a server would say. Plainer words are easier for a new hire to say aloud.
findings.fix: the flour dried pasta is made from. It gives pasta and bread a firm bite and a golden color.

findings.claim: so run it straight from the pass.
findings.because: 'The pass' is kitchen slang a third-day server may not know yet. Say plainly what to do.
findings.fix: so run it to the table the moment it is up.

findings.claim: It's tiny pasta from North Africa, steamed until light and fluffy.
findings.because: Couscous is the classic grain-bowl mix-up: guests take it for a grain like quinoa or rice. The guest line is the part a server says aloud, and it never says wheat. 'Pasta' alone does not tell a guest who avoids wheat what it is made of. The card's own notThis exists because of this confusion.
findings.fix: It's tiny wheat pasta from North Africa, steamed until light and fluffy.

findings.claim: Semolina gnocchi, brown butter, sage
findings.because: Semolina gnocchi (gnocchi alla romana) are classically made with milk, butter, egg yolk and parmesan. madeWith lists only durum wheat, so a server reading this menu line from the card would give an incomplete ingredient picture for the dish shown. A line where semolina is the whole story avoids that.
findings.fix: Semolina bucatini, cacio e pepe

findings.claim: Arborio rice pudding, vanilla, poached pear
findings.because: Rice pudding is made with milk, often cream and sometimes egg, but madeWith lists only rice. A server looking at the card for this menu line would see rice as the only ingredient. The card is about the rice, so use a risotto line instead.
findings.fix: Arborio risotto, spring peas, parmesan

findings.claim: The hard dark hull keeps it chewy
findings.because: The hull (husk) is removed in processing; the dark, chewy layer is the seed coat or bran that stays on the grain. The deck's own wild-rice lexicon entry calls the black layer the bran.
findings.fix: The hard dark bran coat keeps it chewy

findings.claim: a true Asian rice with a dark bran that cooks soft and sticky
findings.because: Most black rice sold as 'forbidden rice' is not glutinous and cooks up chewy, not sticky. Only the Thai black sticky kind is glutinous.
findings.fix: a true Asian rice whose dark color sits in its bran

findings.claim: semolina
findings.because: Semolina is durum wheat. A guest with a wheat allergy, or a new server, may not know that, and this list is the card's only allergy flag.
findings.fix: durum wheat semolina

findings.claim: semolina
findings.because: Semolina is durum wheat. On the only list that works as an allergy flag, the word wheat should appear.
findings.fix: durum wheat semolina

findings.claim: Best of all floating in a rich, clear broth, a Bologna winter dish.
findings.because: A verbless fragment that a nervous new hire will stumble over aloud. 'Best of all' also sounds like the server is steering the guest toward a broth dish that may not be what this menu serves, since tortellini often come with cream or butter sauces.
findings.fix: In Bologna they come floating in a rich, clear broth.

findings.claim: Short curled shells of eggless semolina dough, pressed by a finger
findings.because: Every word here also fits the neighbouring Orecchiette card: eggless semolina, pressed by a finger or thumb, and 'curled' or 'shell' for a cupped piece. A test taker could accept this gist for Orecchiette. The shape that tells cavatelli apart is a small hollow roll, like a tiny hot dog bun.
findings.fix: Short eggless semolina curls shaped like tiny hot dog buns

findings.claim: They're little curled shells of hand-pressed pasta
findings.because: Guests hear 'shells' as the familiar shell pasta, conchiglie, which is a different shape. The hot dog bun picture is the one servers actually use and it tells the guest what will land on the plate.
findings.fix: They're little hand-rolled pasta curls from southern Italy, like tiny hot dog buns. Dense and chewy, and the hollow holds sauce.

findings.claim: Short curled shells of eggless semolina dough, pressed by a finger
findings.because: "Eggless" tells the reader the pasta has no egg. A server will repeat that to a guest with an egg allergy. Many American kitchens make cavatelli from a flour and ricotta dough, and some add egg. Describe what the dough is made with, not what it leaves out.
findings.fix: Short curled shells of semolina and water dough, pressed by a finger

findings.claim: Durum semolina with no egg gives a firm, chewy bite
findings.because: "With no egg" is an absence claim a guest could rely on, and house recipes vary: ricotta versions are common and some add egg. The mechanism holds if you name the flour.
findings.fix: Durum semolina and water give a firm, chewy bite

findings.claim: These are firm pasta, no potato.
findings.because: "No potato" is another claim that the dish lacks something, and regional potato cavatelli do exist. Tell the two apart by texture instead.
findings.fix: These are firm pasta, not soft dumplings.

findings.claim: "semolina", "sometimes ricotta"
findings.because: Many guests with a wheat allergy do not know semolina is wheat, and the house form for this is "wheat flour". Ricotta doughs also sometimes take egg, which the list leaves out.
findings.fix: "durum wheat semolina", "sometimes ricotta", "sometimes egg"

findings.claim: Small cupped disks of eggless durum dough, thin in the middle
findings.because: "Eggless" is a free-from claim about egg that a server could pass on as an assurance. Recipes vary by kitchen. Name the dough instead.
findings.fix: Small cupped disks of semolina and water dough, thin in the middle

findings.claim: It is eggless semolina dough, dragged by knife and shaped over a thumb.
findings.because: The trap's explanation makes the same no-egg claim, and this is what the reader learns as the right answer. Say what the dough is made with.
findings.fix: It is semolina and water dough, dragged by knife and shaped over a thumb.

findings.claim: "semolina"
findings.because: A guest with a wheat allergy may not know semolina is durum wheat. Name the wheat, as the other pasta cards do with "wheat flour".
findings.fix: "durum wheat semolina"

findings.claim: "mortadella"
findings.because: Mortadella, including the Bologna IGP product, is often studded with pistachio. That puts a tree nut into a classic tortellini filling. A server needs that flagged for a guest with a nut allergy.
findings.fix: "mortadella", "sometimes pistachio"

findings.claim: The Agnolotti trap reads "Long flat ribbons of fresh egg pasta, cut by hand and tossed in ragu". That is a true description of Tagliatelle (fd_0185), and nearly repeats its gist. A trap may not be true of another card on the roster.
findings.because: The Agnolotti trap reads "Long flat ribbons of fresh egg pasta, cut by hand and tossed in ragu". That is a true description of Tagliatelle (fd_0185), and nearly repeats its gist. A trap may not be true of another card on the roster.
findings.fix: Replace it with a false description in the same length band (60 to 72 chars) that fits no roster card, e.g. "Large baked tubes of dried pasta, stuffed with ricotta and spinach" (66). Why: "They are small pinched pockets of fresh egg pasta, boiled and never baked."

findings.claim: The Cavatelli notThis contradicts its own why. It says "These are firm pasta, not soft dumplings", while the why says "more like a dumpling than a noodle". It also restates the dumpling point twice and never addresses Orecchiette, which is listed in confusedWithTerms.
findings.because: The Cavatelli notThis contradicts its own why. It says "These are firm pasta, not soft dumplings", while the why says "more like a dumpling than a noodle". It also restates the dumpling point twice and never addresses Orecchiette, which is listed in confusedWithTerms.
findings.fix: notThis: "Not gnocchi, which are soft potato dumplings, and not orecchiette, which are round cupped ears. These are short curls with a slit."

findings.claim: The Gnocchi guest line says "turned into bite-size pasta" while its notThis opens "Not rolled pasta". A server gets told two opposite things. Gnocchi also has no link to Cavatelli, although Cavatelli lists Gnocchi in confusedWithTerms.
findings.because: The Gnocchi guest line says "turned into bite-size pasta" while its notThis opens "Not rolled pasta". A server gets told two opposite things. Gnocchi also has no link to Cavatelli, although Cavatelli lists Gnocchi in confusedWithTerms.
findings.fix: Guest: "They're soft little potato dumplings, light and pillowy. Think of the best mashed potato shaped into bite-size pieces." Add "Cavatelli" to seeAlsoTerms (or confusedWithTerms, with notThis naming it).

findings.claim: The guest line "Despite the name it's no kin to wheat" works as an implied free-from verdict at the table. The packet row for this term said "gluten free alternative", and the card's own note says soba, blini and crepes are often blended with wheat flour. A guest who asks about wheat hears "no wheat". The trap "An old variety of whole wheat, roasted dark" also sits close to Freekeh (roasted wheat) and Farro (ancient wheat).
findings.because: The guest line "Despite the name it's no kin to wheat" works as an implied free-from verdict at the table. The packet row for this term said "gluten free alternative", and the card's own note says soba, blini and crepes are often blended with wheat flour. A guest who asks about wheat hears "no wheat". The trap "An old variety of whole wheat, roasted dark" also sits close to Freekeh (roasted wheat) and Farro (ancient wheat).
findings.fix: Guest: "It's the dark, earthy seed of a plant related to rhubarb, ground into flour for crepes and noodles. It tastes toasty, a bit like dark rye." Leave the not-a-grass fact to the why. Consider a trap such as "A dark variety of rye, ground coarse for a sour, malty taste" (60).

findings.claim: The Risotto note says "the moment" twice in two sentences, and its first sentence says the same thing as its second.
findings.because: The Risotto note says "the moment" twice in two sentences, and its first sentence says the same thing as its second.

findings.because: Farro lists Freekeh in confusedWithTerms, but its notThis addresses only barley and piccolo. Freekeh lists Farro only as seeAlso, so the link is one-sided and the confusion is weak.

findings.because: Semolina lists Polenta in confusedWithTerms (yellow and gritty), but Polenta does not link back.

critic.notes: The section mean is 669 characters of prose per card (ceiling 720). The longest cards are fd_0180 (752), fd_0179 (734) and fd_0188 (732), all under 900. Every roster row has a card, and no row carries a knownPacketError. I found no em or en dashes, no banned substrings and no verdict words. Every gist and trap stays free of its own mayNotAppear words. Across the 17 cards with traps, gists average 62.6 characters and traps 62.4, so length gives nothing away. Cross-section links look right: Grits and Hominy are linked, Wild Rice points to Carolina Gold Rice, Buckwheat to Galette, and Couscous to Semolina. findings.claim: "rice", "often butter", "often parmesan"
findings.because: The list already describes the finished risotto because it names butter and parmesan, so it should also flag what a classic risotto is built on. That means white wine, which is alcohol, added after the toast, and the broth, which may be chicken, meat or fish. A guest avoiding alcohol or fish would otherwise get no flag.

findings.claim: A two-part wooden stamp, often pearwood, cuts each disk and presses a design into both sides at once.
findings.because: The cutting and the stamping are two separate steps. The hollow cutter end of the stamp cuts the disk first. The disk is then pressed between the two carved halves, which emboss both faces together. As written, the sentence reads as if one motion does both.
findings.fix: A wooden stamp, often pearwood, cuts each disk, then its two halves press a design into both sides.

findings.claim: It's Piedmont's hand-cut egg pasta, made with almost nothing but yolks, so it's golden and silky. In the fall it carries shaved white truffle.
findings.because: The guest line never says the pasta is thin, and thinness is what sets it apart from tagliatelle, so the guest still does not know what arrives. 'Hand-cut' promises something many kitchens do not do, because tajarin is often cut by machine. 'In the fall it carries shaved white truffle' sounds like the truffle comes with the dish, when it is usually a costly supplement.
findings.fix: It's thin egg pasta from Piedmont, made with almost all yolks, so it's golden and silky. In the fall it's the classic base for white truffle.

All 33 roster rows have a card: 28 are already live in src/lib/data/floor-deck.json and the 5 new ones are in this batch. No knownPacketError exists in this section's brief. I found no verdict words, banned substrings or dashes. Every new card has a say and a level, every guest line answers 'what is that?', and every trap is within 10 characters of its gist without the gist being the longest option. Prose totals per card: Tajarin 702, Uovo 813, Corzetti 600, Vialone 671, Middlins 745. The 28 existing cards average 669.9, all 33 average 675.4 (ceiling 720) and the new five average 706.2.

Reverse links the operator should add, if the build does not mirror confusedWith on its own:
- Tagliatelle to Tajarin
- Ravioli to Uovo in Raviolo
- Carnaroli and Arborio to Vialone Nano
- Grits to Middlins (the Grits card currently lists only Polenta and Hominy)
- seeAlso from Carolina Gold to Middlins

Optional tightening, not gate failures:
(1) Uovo in Raviolo is the longest card (813). Its note restates the why's last clause ('the yolk just warms, so it runs'). Keep the note, because it is the real raw-service fact, and trim the why sentence to 'It boils for only 2 to 3 minutes, so the yolk stays runny.'
(2) Corzetti origin states as fact that the name comes from the 14th-century Genoese corzetto coin. A competing derivation exists (croxetti, 'little crosses', from the cross stamped on them, which is the alias the card already lists). Consider 'probably named for...' or 'often said to be named for...'.
(3) Tajarin's 'no wider than about 2 millimeters' is fine with the hedge. Many sources give 2 to 3 mm, so 'about 2 to 3 millimeters' is the safer wording.
(4) Watch Tajarin against Chitarra. Both are thin fresh egg strands, so a seeAlso link is worth adding; it is not a confusion.
